We also have obtained a comprehensive database of diverse technologies that we are using to conduct studies that determine best pathways to follow and under different market and scenarios. We have also built a comprehensive database based on a survey of MRFs in the United States, that provides insights into feedstocks that they manage, their economies of scale, and their economic models (Bradshaw et al., 2025); this database can be relevant in informing policy that accelerates the deployment of infrastructure for better sorting plastic waste (which impacts further chemical recycling). The survey performed by Bradshaw et al details the number, scale, feedstock capability, and unrecyclable residue content of MRFs across all regions in the U.S. Topic Area 2 – Characterization, Logistics, and Rheology of Mixed Plastic Streams Solvent Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP) has emerged as a practical, high selectivity route to recover constituent polymers from multilayer flexible packaging—one of the most problematic waste streams for mechanical recycling due to immiscible resin combinations and engineered barrier layers. In a foundational study by the ISU team, polymers produced by STRAP from two multilayer films showed that the recovered polymers maintained molecular weight comparable to the virgin precursors, while thermal property changes were largely attributable to reversible solvent retention effects (e.g., depressed glass transition temperatures that recovered after enhanced drying) (Cecon et al., 2022). Heavy metals (Cd, Cr, Pb) were not detected in the recovered resins, supporting potential regulatory compatibility in downstream applications. These results indicate that dissolution precipitation can deliver clean, specification aligned resin streams from laminates that are otherwise destined for landfill or energy recovery. Critically, performance retention was independently corroborated via rheology. The UMass-Amherst team compared STRAP-recycled polyethylenes (PE) with virgin PE using small-amplitude oscillatory shear, steady-shear viscosity, and extensional rheology, all performed under carefully established thermally stable conditions (using time-resolved sweeps to bound viable test windows) (Tillinghast et al., 2024). They found shear and extensional responses of STRAP PE closely track virgin PE, consistent with preserved entanglement density and molecular-weight distributions needed for high-performance blown-film and cast-film operations. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry of solvent washes showed contaminants removed during STRAP, aligning with the mechanical integrity observed in rheology. Together, these findings support positioning STRAP as a “quality-first” chemical recycling approach for multilayer films, complementing mechanical routes where homopolymer streams are available and relatively clean. On the supply side, MRF #3–7 bales in the U.S. are highly variable, with composition and contamination profiles changing substantially between facilities and seasons, as documented by the ISU team through labor-intensive manual sorting, ATR-FTIR identification, and downstream processing/characterization of recovered resins (Cecon et al., 2024).
